papers.title: Biointerface-Customized Nanomodulators Induce Mitochondria-Specific Dysfunction to Reprogram Tumor Immunity.
papers.authors: Zhen X, Chen Y, Li L, Zhang T, Li M, Wang R, Sun Y, Li J, Ma S, Zhou R, Wang S, Xie X.
papers.abstract: Tumor mitochondria regulate cancer progression and immune evasion. However, current therapeutic strategies lack the subcellular precision required to selectively induce immune-beneficial mitochondrial dysfunction without causing systemic toxicity. Here, we report a biointerface-customized nanomodulator (C/C-HP@M2M-TPP), developed through a biointerface-engineered strategy (BES), that integrates sequential targeting and controlled activation to induce mitochondria-specific dysfunction and reprogram tumor immunity. Through a customized biointerface coating, the nanomodulators achieve preferential tumor accumulation and mitochondria-directed subcellular localization. Co-delivered calcium ion donors and efflux inhibitors cooperatively induce mitochondrial ion interference and dysfunction, which is further amplified by photothermal activation. This localized mitochondrial interference promotes immunogenic cell death and robust antitumor immune activation, resulting in potent tumor regression in mice. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic analyses further identify mitochondrial disruption as a key mechanistic driver of tumor immune reprogramming. This work establishes biointerface-customized nanomodulation as a subcellular immunomodulatory therapeutic strategy in vivo.

papers.title: OpenAntigens: a structure-aware database for antigen construct design across the human cell-surface and secreted proteome.
papers.authors: Teixeira AAR, Zhu H, Kothiwal D, Cao R, Mills A.
papers.abstract: Choosing which region of a protein to express remains poorly standardized in antibody discovery, recombinant reagent generation, structural biology, and computational binder design. For human cell-surface and secreted proteins, this requires reconciling topology, processing, predicted, and experimental structure, modifications, interaction partners, orthologs, paralogs, and cross-reactivity risk before ordering DNA. OpenAntigens is a free, no-login database of construct-design reports for 5328 human secreted, GPI-anchored, single-pass, and multipass proteins. It integrates UniProt topology, AlphaFold pLDDT and PAE, PDB precedent, InterPro and Pfam domains, mouse and cynomolgus orthologs, paralog and family context, Open Targets disease associations, partner and assembly context, and BLAST searches. It provides 55 305 construct suggestions spanning full design regions, PDB-backed boundaries, annotated domains, pLDDT/PAE-derived regions, and membrane-expression options, plus 148 722 sequence-similarity hits to help choose constructs and assess cross-reactivity. For targets with compatible AlphaFold models, the interactive designer links sequence, structure, pLDDT, and PAE, allowing users to revise boundaries and export species-equivalent sequences with real-time cysteine and modification warnings. OpenAntigens places reproducible construct suggestions, comparative context, and browser editing in one workflow, reducing manual reconciliation across resources. OpenAntigens is available at openantigens.org.

papers.title: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived spheroids and microtissues for biofabrication: advances in bioassembly and bioprinting strategies.
papers.authors: Contreras-Pérez DA, Hoffmann A, Egger D.
papers.abstract: Biofabrication integrates biological and engineering principles to generate functional tissues for regenerative medicine, drug screening, and disease modeling. Among the diverse cellular sources available, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a critical component due to their multipotency, immunomodulatory capacity, and scalability. This review focuses on MSC-derived spheroids and microtissues as building blocks for biofabrication, organizing recent advances in bioassembly and bioprinting strategies around the axis of undifferentiated versus pre-differentiated microtissues and how the timing of differentiation shapes construct functionality. Key technological innovations, including dynamic culture systems, scaffold-free assembly, and high-resolution bioprinting (e.g. droplet-based), have enabled enhanced control over microtissue maturation and structural fidelity. The role of the cellular microenvironment in determining MSC fate is examined, emphasizing how biochemical cues, mechanical properties, and oxygen gradients can be engineered during microtissue formation. Cellular heterogeneity is addressed as a path-dependent variable continuously reshaped by donor-specific factors (age, sex, health status) and process-imposed cues (isolation methods, expansion conditions, and mechanical stress) throughout the in vitro life cycle, and concrete mitigation strategies are discussed, including prospective cell sorting and a proposed functional potency panel (extracellular matrix deposition, fusion competence, and secretome profiling), alongside recent advancements in automated and machine learning-based biofabrication platforms. Vascularization and immunological integration are examined as central translation bottlenecks, covering endothelial co-culture, prevascularized spheroids, sacrificial bioprinting, and MSC-driven modulation of the host immune response. By integrating the fabrication route, heterogeneity as a manufacturing process variable, and translational/regulatory bottlenecks into a single framework, this review highlights recent advances, discusses current limitations, and outlines future directions for clinical translation of MSC-based biofabrication.

papers.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression.
papers.authors: Cuomo ASE, Spenceley E, Tanudisastro HA, Bowen B, Henry A, Huang HL, Xue A, Zhou W, Welland MJ, Bryen SJ, Dong OA, Lee AS, Pullin JM, Wing K, Tang O, Gray MP, Franklin M, Harper M, Silk M, Bobowik K, Stuckey A, Marshall J, Bakiris V, Uren C, McCloy RA, Madala BS, Miniter A, Bartie C, Neavin DR, Qiao Z, Ben-David E, Chen L, Farh KK, Grieve SM, Nguyen T, Wallace C, Piscionere J, Siggs OM, Nicholas H, de Lange KM, Hewitt AW, Figtree GA, MacArthur DG, Powell JE.
papers.abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases 1,2 . Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues 3 . Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

papers.title: Effects of post-transplant cyclophosphamide on immune reconstitution after haploidentical and HLA-matched transplant.
papers.authors: Ansuinelli M, Kim HT, Malfona F, Ikegawa S, Panaro KM, Gervais C, Tamada R, Reynolds CG, Shapiro RM, Gooptu M, Kelkar AH, Nageshwar PK, Romee R, Nikiforow S, Koreth J, Ho VT, Cutler CS, Antin JH, Wu CJ, Kean LS, Soiffer RJ, Ritz J.
papers.abstract: Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) is increasingly used for graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis in both HLA-matched (matched-PTCy) and haplotype-mismatched (haplo-PTCy) hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT), but the effects of PTCy on immune reconstitution in different donor settings remain incompletely characterized. We analyzed immune reconstitution in 210 adult patients undergoing haplo-PTCy, matched-PTCy, or HLA-matched HCT using tacrolimus/methotrexate (matched-CNI) for GVHD prophylaxis. Both PTCy cohorts also received tacrolimus/mycophenolate mofetil (Tac/MMF). Reconstitution of T, B, NK and dendritic-cell subsets in serial blood samples was monitored using flow cytometry and a panel of 37 cell surface markers. T cell receptor (TCRVb) sequencing was used to assess repertoire diversity in purified CD4Treg, CD4Tcon, and CD8 T cell populations. Early recovery of T, B, NK and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, was delayed in both PTCy cohorts compared with matched-CNI with more pronounced delays after haplo-PTCy. Delayed recovery after PTCy primarily involved naïve CD4 and CD8 T-cell subsets and naïve B-cell populations. Recovery of NK-T cells and γδT cells was delayed for more than 1 year in both PTCy groups. T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing revealed delayed recovery of repertoire diversity after haplo-PTCy compared to matched-CNI but not after matched-PTCy. CD8 clonality remained elevated at later time points after haplo-PTCy, suggesting more persistent repertoire restriction in this setting. Overall, these findings identify multiple effects of GVHD prophylaxis with PTCy on immune reconstitution. However, immune recovery is more rapid and T cell receptor repertoire diversity better preserved when recipient and donor are HLA-matched.

papers.title: Downregulation of SIRT3 Activates Macrophage Proinflammatory Function and Exacerbates Olfactory Loss in a Mouse Model of Chronic Rhinosinusitis.
papers.authors: Wang T, Yan J, Cheng Y, Cha X, Li F, Li T, Cai B, Zhou M, Liang C, Wang Z, Fu P, Wang S, Xie Y, Xiong C, Xu Z, Chen L, Gao A, Qu Z, Zhu Y, Yu Y, Zhuang C, Wang E, Peng H, Ren W, Liu H.
papers.abstract: Background Inflammation of the olfactory mucosa, rather than airflow obstruction, is a major barrier to olfactory recovery in chronic rhinosinusitis with olfactory dysfunction (CRSwOD). Macrophages, a predominant immune cell population in the olfactory mucosa, play a key role in regulating local inflammation and olfactory neuroregeneration. Objective This study aimed to investigate the role of Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) in modulating macrophage function and its impact on olfactory recovery in CRSwOD. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics data were analyzed to characterize immune and neuronal alterations in CRSwOD, with a focus on macrophage activation states. In vivo experiments using SIRT3-deficient mice were performed to evaluate olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) integrity, while in vitro assays examined the metabolic and inflammatory profiles of SIRT3-deficient macrophages under inflammatory conditions. Results Transcriptomic analysis revealed that olfactory dysfunction was closely associated with the altered functional status of mucosal macrophages. During the progression of chronic rhinosinusitis in mice, loss of SIRT3 exacerbated OSN loss and impaired the protective role of macrophages in maintaining neuronal homeostasis. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deficiency enhanced macrophage proinflammatory activity, increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) expression, promoted glycolysis, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential. Conclusion In a mouse model of chronic rhinosinusitis, SIRT3 modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory metabolism within the olfactory mucosa, thereby protecting against inflammation-induced olfactory damage. These findings provide mechanistic insight into inflammation-driven olfactory dysfunction and identify SIRT3 as a potential therapeutic target for CRSwOD.
papers.venue: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology

papers.title: Macrophage biology and immunoregulation in health and disease.
papers.authors: Zhao H, Chou YJ, Huang SC.
papers.abstract: Macrophages are versatile immune cells that maintain tissue homeostasis and shape disease progression through continuous adaptation to the local environment. Recent advances in single-cell, spatial, and multiomics technologies have revealed extensive diversity in tissue-specific macrophage identities and their adaptation to physiological and pathological contexts. Emerging evidence indicates that macrophage behavior emerges from the coordinated integration of ontogenetic imprinting, environmental sensing, metabolic rewiring, and epigenetic remodeling. These interconnected layers collectively determine macrophage responses in inflammatory diseases, neurodegeneration, and cancer, creating both challenges and opportunities for therapeutic intervention. In this review, we provide an overview of recent mechanistic insights into the molecular circuits governing macrophage plasticity and function and discuss how this evolving framework can inform next-generation macrophage-based therapeutic strategies to restore immune homeostasis and improve disease outcomes.

papers.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression.
papers.authors: Tanudisastro HA, Cuomo ASE, Weisburd B, Welland M, Spenceley E, Franklin M, Xue A, Huang HL, Bowen B, Fan J, Dong OA, Henry A, Allen PC, Wing K, Tang O, Gray M, Reis ALM, Margoliash J, Kurtas NE, Pullin JM, Lee AS, Brand H, Harper M, Bobowik K, Silk M, Miniter A, Marshall J, Bakiris V, Madala BS, Uren C, Bartie C, McCloy RA, Senabouth A, Dashnow H, Fearnley L, Martin-Trujillo A, Dolzhenko E, Qiao Z, Grieve SM, Nguyen T, Ben-David E, Chen L, Farh KK, Talkowski ME, Alexander SI, Siggs OM, Gruenschloss L, Nicholas HR, Piscionere J, Simons C, Wallace C, Gymrek M, Deveson IW, Hewitt AW, Figtree GA, de Lange KM, Powell JE, MacArthur DG.
papers.abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs)-highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome-are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis 1 . Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts 2 , and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals 3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

papers.title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk.
papers.authors: Xue A, Fan J, Dong OA, Huang HL, Chen L, Allen PC, Spenceley E, Sagi-Zsigmond E, Bowen B, Henry A, Cuomo ASE, Tanudisastro HA, Qiao Z, Dorans E, Ben-David E, Farh KK, Hu L, Liu YC, Neavin DR, Lee AS, Senabouth A, Bartie C, McCloy RA, Chin V, Zhou W, Price AL, de Lange KM, Figtree GA, Hewitt AW, MacArthur DG, Powell JE.
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms 1 , but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data 2-4 . Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells) 5 defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5-22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study-eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL-cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4 + T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk.

papers.title: Identification of ageing-related genes in prostate cancer with type 2 Diabetes using machine learning: a multi-omics study focusing on SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4.
papers.authors: Zhang W, Zhang X, Zhang C, Shi X, Deng Y, Gao Y, Bi K, Wang Z, Chen G, Ye Z, An Z, Fu W.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) demonstrates complex associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and ageing, though their interconnected molecular mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify and validate diagnostic biomarkers at the intersection of these pathways to enable early detection and risk stratification in high-risk populations. Bioinformatic analysis was performed on PCa and T2DM transcriptomic data downloaded from the GEO database, followed by differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment. Eight machine learning algorithms were applied to identify hub ageing-related genes (ARGs), with SHAP analysis interpreting feature importance. A nomogram model was constructed and validated across multiple cohorts. Immune infiltration, drug sensitivity, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics were used for mechanistic exploration. Three key ARGs (SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4) were identified and used to develop a diagnostic model with high accuracy (AUCs: 0.726-0.905). SOX4 promoted immune evasion, PRNP exhibited context-dependent duality, and FOXO4 functioned as a tumor suppressor. Spatial and single-cell analyses revealed cell-type-specific expression and fibroblast-epithelial communication via MIF, LRP1, and FZD1. Drug sensitivity profiling identified abiraterone and docetaxel as potential therapeutics for high- and low-risk patients, respectively. In conclusion, SOX4, PRNP, and FOXO4 are key biomarkers linking PCa, T2DM, and ageing, and the diagnostic model shows robust performance and clinical utility, providing insights into microenvironment-driven mechanisms and personalized treatment strategies for PCa patients with T2DM.

papers.title: B cell subsets are associated with durable responses in distinct cancer types after immune checkpoint inhibition.
papers.authors: Kim SS, Miyauchi S, Jones RN, Weihe E, Zhang L, Murtadha J, Ryan ST, Kato S, Kurzrock R, Sicklick JK, Cohen EEW, Patel SP, Boles SG, Gold KA, Botta GP, Patel H, Shatsky RA, Kaech SM, Roy S, Sanders PD, Murphy JD, Kane CJ, Pittman EI, Zou J, Pu M, Quach NE, Gutkind JS, Messer K, Simeone D, Mell LK, Califano JA, Jamieson C, Mundt AJ, Sharabi AB.
papers.abstract: B cells are a critical arm of the adaptive immune system. However, the impact of B cells and antibody responses on overall cancer survival remains understudied. Here, we report results from a prospective randomized phase 2 trial of 106 patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and identify that B cell antibody responses are associated with exceptional complete responses to ICI in certain cancer types. To further dissect the impact of B cell subtypes, we generated a comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing database of intratumoral B cells in 12 tumor types from 152 patients. We found a context-dependent role for B cells, in which they are beneficial in certain cancer types and potentially unfavorable in others, with germinal center and memory B cells enriched in favorable prognosis cohorts and immunoglobulin A-positive plasma cells enriched in unfavorable prognosis cohorts. Depletion of B cells using rituximab in patients before surgery affected intratumoral T cell frequency and diversity. Furthermore, we show that B cells improve long-term overall survival even when T cell infiltrates are already high, indicating that a coordinated dual-arm T cell and B cell adaptive immune response is key to long-term tumor control. Overall, these results demonstrate that B cells and antibody responses in the proper context play an important role in durable complete responses in multiple tumor types.

papers.title: Deficiency of NBAS causes immune dysregulation due to hyperactivation of IFN signaling.
papers.authors: Liu C, Zhang L, Lu M, Shen Y, Yao Y, Liu F, Wang Q, Zhang B, Guo L, Li X, Zhou Q, Mao J, Yu X.
papers.abstract: NBAS deficiency is a multisystem disorder, but its immunologic manifestations and underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. Here, we expand the genotypic and phenotypic spectrum of NBAS deficiency through four patients carrying five loss-of-function NBAS mutations. Minigene assays and RNA analysis showed that these splicing or missense mutations resulted in aberrant alternative splicing. Clinically, the patients showed early-onset recurrent or persistent cytopenias and immune dysregulation, together with severe infections, inflammatory activation, and multi-organ involvement, including renal and neurologic manifestations. Transcriptomic analysis revealed overactivation of type I interferon signaling pathways compared with healthy controls, and single-cell RNA sequencing demonstrated that this upregulated inflammation was predominantly driven by myeloid cells. Together, these findings identify NBAS deficiency as a cause of immune dysregulation characterized by myeloid-driven type I interferonopathy, expand the clinical spectrum of NBAS-related disorders, and highlight the critical role of NBAS in maintaining immune homeostasis.

papers.title: RAD51 expression in pan-cancer and its prognostic and immune mechanisms in glioma.
papers.authors: Hou L, Wang Y, Zhan X, Li J, Zhang Z, Cai W, Su L, Han W, Han X, Han Y, Lv X, Xue X, Zhou H.
papers.abstract: Objective Glioma is a heterogeneous, malignant intracranial tumor with dismal prognosis, lacking effective diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers. The DNA repair gene RAD51 participates in tumor progression, while its clinical function and immune regulatory mechanism in glioma remain undefined. This study aimed to clarify RAD51's expression features, clinical significance and immunomodulatory role in glioma. Methods Data from TCGA, CGGA325 and CGGA693 glioma cohorts were utilized to analyze RAD51 expression, its links with clinicopathological features and prognosis. ROC curve, survival analysis, Cox regression and nomogram modeling were performed for clinical evaluation. Multiple bioinformatics analyses were conducted to explore tumor immune microenvironment regulation, and clinical specimens were used for protein expression verification. Results RAD51 was markedly overexpressed in glioma and pan-cancers, correlated with elevated tumor stemness and poor prognosis. Its high expression was associated with advanced age, higher WHO grade, IDH wild-type and 1p/19q non-codeletion. With an AUC of 0.960, RAD51 showed excellent diagnostic efficacy and was an independent adverse prognostic factor. The validated nomogram achieved accurate risk prediction. Mechanistically, high RAD51 was associated with an immunosuppressive microenvironment and correlated with increased infiltration of Th2 cells and macrophages.Nineteen core RAD51-related immune genes were identified and linked to poor prognosis. Clinical tests confirmed upregulated RAD51 protein in high-grade gliomas. Conclusion RAD51 is a robust diagnostic biomarker and independent prognostic risk factor for glioma. It is correlated with glioma malignant features and shows potential links to altered immune-gene expression and immunosuppressive microenvironment. The nomogram supports clinical risk stratification, providing novel targets for glioma prognosis evaluation and immunotherapy.

papers.title: Integrative characterization of cell-surface proximity interactions using DTSSP crosslinking and high-dimensional profiling.
papers.authors: Thu MM, Takheaw N, Laopajon W, Kasinrerk W, Pata S.
papers.abstract: Extracellular protein interactions mediated by cell surface receptors are fundamental to intercellular communication and immune regulation. Identifying novel ligand-receptor interactions helps uncover previously unknown signalling pathways and improves understanding of immune mechanisms. In this study, we introduce a methodology aimed at facilitating the detection of cell-surface binding or proximity through flow cytometry. We demonstrate the efficacy of employing DTSSP (3,3'-dithiobis sulfosuccinimidylpropionate) crosslinking in conjunction with high-dimensional flow cytometry to achieve enhanced detection of cell-surface association while preserving the integrity of single-cell immune profiling. This strategy provides a versatile methodological framework for studying cell-surface interactions across heterogeneous immune cell populations.

papers.title: cGAS-STING activation promotes abdominal aortic aneurysm formation in mice and humans: Therapeutic potential of inhibition.
papers.authors: Du P, Ma X, Zhu F, Zhu G, Li F, Nie H, Yu M, Tang L, Yan J, Li Y, Sun Y, Huang K, Yang H, Feng J.
papers.abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a life-threatening vascular disease lacking effective pharmacotherapy. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) innate immune pathway has been linked to inflammatory conditions, yet its role in AAA remains unclear. Here, we combined single-cell transcriptomics, mouse models, pharmacological inhibition, and human tissue validation to investigate the role of this pathway in AAA. In murine single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, cGAS-STING activation was predominantly observed in AAA endothelial cells (ECs). Human scRNA-seq and scissor-based classification of stable versus ruptured AAAs showed that cGAS and STING1 were significantly upregulated in ECs from ruptured AAA, implicating pathway activation in rupture risk. Bioinformatic analyses suggested that endothelial cGAS-STING activation correlates with barrier dysfunction and oxidative stress, and that dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) deficiency may link DNA damage to pathway activation. In Angiotensin II (Ang II) -induced murine AAA, cGAS, p-STING, and p-TBK1 were markedly elevated. Pharmacological blockade with RU.521 (cGAS inhibitor) or STING-IN-2 (STING antagonist) reduced AAA incidence, aortic dilation, and structural damage, while improving endothelial mitochondrial morphology. In human AAA tissues, immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed increased cGAS, STING, and TBK1 expression. Moreover, RU.521 or STING-IN-2 treatment of patient-derived 3D AAA organoids significantly downregulated cGAS, p-STING, and p-TBK1, confirming target engagement. Collectively, our findings indicate that the cGAS-STING pathway is activated in murine and human AAA, and that targeting this axis may offer a promising therapeutic approach to limit AAA progression.

papers.title: Myeloid Suppressor Cells Drive HCC Invasiveness via the THBS1-SDC4 Pathway.
papers.authors: Liu S, Gu J, Sheng S, Zhang S, Fei Z, Li C, Hu K, Jiang C, Bu F, Qin X, Xu Q, Xu Z, Sun B, Xia A.
papers.abstract: Background & aims Monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) accumulate in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but their activation and tumor-promoting mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated how stromal-myeloid-tumor crosstalk promotes HCC invasiveness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Methods We analyzed single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 36 HCC patients and spatial transcriptomics data from 2 HCC specimens to characterize M-MDSC localization and intercellular signaling. Matrix cancer-associated fibroblast and M-MDSC phenotypes and interactions were assessed using molecular and functional assays. Thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling was investigated in xenografts in immunodeficient mice (n = 8/group) and diethylnitrosamine/carbon tetrachloride-induced HCC in the immunocompetent mice (n = 6/group). Results M-MDSCs preferentially localized to EMT-active tumor margins and correlated with EMT activity (Spearman r = 0.30; false discovery rate = 3.3 × 10 -4 ) and shorter overall survival (log-rank P = 0.00124). Matrix cancer-associated fibroblasts promoted M-MDSC activation through collagen-associated CD44 signaling. Activated M-MDSCs induced EMT through thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling, whereas syndecan-4 deficiency suppressed tumor cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and EMT. Thrombospondin-1-deficient M-MDSCs reduced xenograft progression and increased interferon-γ-positive CD8 + T-cell infiltration and cytotoxic immune markers in immunocompetent HCC. A thrombospondin communication pathway score was associated with shorter overall survival (log-rank P = 2.28 × 10 -5 ; Cox hazard ratio = 1.23, P = 0.0193). Conclusions Matrix cancer-associated fibroblasts promote monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cell activation, driving epithelial-mesenchymal transition in hepatocellular carcinoma through thrombospondin-1-syndecan-4 signaling. Targeting this axis may restrain tumor progression and enhance antitumor immunity. Impact and implications This study provides mechanistic insight into how M-MDSCs are activated within the HCC tumor microenvironment and subsequently drive tumor cell EMT through THBS1-SDC4 signaling. These findings highlight the importance of tumor-immune-stromal crosstalk in HCC progression and provide a mechanistic framework for understanding the pro-tumor functions of M-MDSCs. The THBS1-SDC4 axis may represent a therapeutically targetable pathway to restrain M-MDSC-mediated tumor aggressiveness and modulate the tumor microenvironment. Further validation in independent clinical cohorts and assessment of therapeutic efficacy are warranted to determine its translational potential.

papers.title: HDAC3 inhibition alleviates neuroinflammation and white matter injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage through modulation of BDNF/TrkB/NF-κB signaling.
papers.authors: Yang H, Hu Z, Zhuang H, Chen S, Zhou S, Sun M, Lian L, Zhou C, Gao X, Huang Y.
papers.abstract: White matter injury (WMI) is a major contributor to neurological deficits after subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is an established modulator of inflammatory responses, yet its contribution to post-SAH white matter pathology remains poorly understood. We used a rat endovascular perforation model and treated animals with RGFP966, a selective HDAC3 inhibitor. Clinical data, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and transmission electron microscopy were integrated to evaluate cellular remodeling and structural integrity. Short- and long-term neurological recovery was assessed using a systematic battery of behavioral tests, while the underlying BDNF/TrkB/NF-κB signaling axis was validated through gain- and loss-of-function experiments. HDAC3 levels were elevated in both the CSF of SAH patients and rat brain tissues, inversely correlating with myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. RGFP966 treatment effectively preserved WMI, evidenced by reduced axonal injury and improved myelin shielding, and translated to superior long-term cognitive performance. ScRNA-seq analysis identified a profound shift in the microglial and oligodendrocyte-lineage landscapes after SAH. HDAC3 inhibition effectively curbed the expansion of pro-inflammatory microglial subsets while restoring homeostatic signatures and enhancing pro-myelination programs. Mechanistically, RGFP966 upregulated BDNF expression and restored TrkB phosphorylation, thereby suppressing NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation. Notably, BDNF knockdown abolished the protective effects of HDAC3 inhibition, whereas exogenous BDNF mimicked the anti-inflammatory and myelin-protective phenotype induced by RGFP966. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that HDAC3 is a pivotal driver of post-SAH neuroinflammation and WMI. Inhibition of HDAC3 exerts neuroprotection by recalibrating the microglial immune microenvironment and restoring the BDNF/TrkB axis.
papers.venue: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics

papers.title: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM): From Genetics to Management.
papers.authors: Papiris SA, Skontzou E, Kolilekas L, Kallieri M, Prountzos S, Athanasopoulou V, Kaltsakas G, Spanou M, Brountzos E, Dinopoulos A, Pujana MA, Manali ED.
papers.abstract: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare multisystem disease that exemplifies how sustained investigation can transform both biological understanding and clinical management. LAM is diagnosed almost exclusively in women, typically during the reproductive years, consistent with an important role for hormonal influences in disease activity. The disease is characterized by diffuse cystic lung remodeling that can lead to progressive loss of lung function and, in severe cases, respiratory failure. Once viewed primarily as an unusual smooth muscle-like proliferation, LAM is now considered a low-grade metastasizing neoplasm characterized by heterogeneous disease-cell states that contribute to remodeling of the lung parenchyma and interact dynamically with stromal, lymphatic, immune, metabolic, and hormonal cues. Although the anatomical origin of LAM cells remains debated and continues to be an active area of research, sporadic and tuberous sclerosis complex-associated LAM (S-LAM and TSC-LAM, respectively) share a central molecular mechanism: biallelic inactivation of TSC1 or TSC2, which disrupts the TSC1-TSC2 protein complex and results in constitutive activation of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). This mechanistic insight provided the rationale for mTORC1 inhibition with sirolimus, which has transformed disease management by stabilizing lung function and reducing disease burden in many patients. In parallel, serum VEGF-D has emerged as a clinically useful biomarker supporting noninvasive diagnosis and the assessment of disease burden and treatment response. Yet current therapies are not curative, and LAM cells persist despite mTORC1 inhibition. Continued advances in single-cell biology, genomic studies, hormonal and metabolic regulation, mechanistic dissection of disease-cell states, immune-stromal interactions, and biomarker discovery are now reshaping LAM as a model of precision medicine for rare neoplastic diseases. These efforts may guide rational combination therapies aimed not only at controlling disease progression but also, ultimately, at eliminating persistent LAM cells.

papers.title: Keratinocyte-derived CHI3L2 reprograms phospholipid metabolism to promote skin inflammation in psoriasis.
papers.authors: Li F, Zhang W, Ma W, Guan Y, Wang Y, Cheng Y, Liang D, Wang Y, Xu X, Feng L, Wang B, Xu J, Mo L, Wang J, Han D, Mou K, Zhou Y, Lu S, Holmdahl R, Meng L, Zhu W.
papers.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by hyperproliferative keratinocytes and a dysregulated cytokine milieu, perpetuating a self-reinforcing inflammatory cycle. Despite the key involvement of keratinocytes in this pathogenic loop, the molecular pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify chitinase-like protein CHI3L2 as a key mediator. Elevated CHI3L2 levels were detected in serum and lesional skin from patients with psoriasis, predominantly in keratinocytes, as also verified by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic analyses. In vitro stimulation of keratinocytes with M5 cytokine cocktail (IL-17A, IL-22, oncostatin M, IL-1α, and TNF-α) increased CHI3L2 expression, demonstrating that CHI3L2 is inducible under inflammatory conditions. Transgenic mice expressing human CHI3L2 exhibited aggravated psoriasis-like phenotypes in both imiquimod- and mannan-induced psoriasis models, characterized by epidermal hyperplasia and scaling. To dissect the role of CHI3L2, we used recombinant protein injection, parabiosis, and bone marrow transplantation, identifying keratinocytes as the primary source of pathogenic CHI3L2. This was further confirmed by keratinocyte-specific CHI3L2 knockin mice. CHI3L2 functions in the HaCaT cell line and primary keratinocytes were investigated by recombinant CHI3L2 administration or CHI3L2 knockout. CHI3L2 disrupted phospholipid homeostasis, leading to altered inflammatory responses, proliferation, and differentiation of keratinocytes. CHI3L2 activated secretory phospholipase A2, elevating lysophosphatidylcholine, thereby establishing an autocrine loop perpetuating keratinocyte inflammation and reshaping the immune microenvironment. Therapeutic neutralization of CHI3L2 with antibodies or intervention of phospholipid pathway ameliorated skin inflammation in mouse psoriasis models. Our findings reveal CHI3L2 as an important regulator of keratinocyte-driven lipid remodeling and inflammation in psoriasis, highlighting potential as a therapeutic target.

papers.title: A cancer-inspired metaheuristic for optimal control of breast cancer treatment.
papers.authors: Ebrahimzadeh A, Khanduzi R, Khandoozi SR, Jajarmi A.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel bio-inspired metaheuristic, referred to as the Cancer Improvement Optimizer (CIO), which is motivated by the fundamental biological processes underlying cancer progression, including tumor proliferation, immune surveillance, therapeutic intervention, dormancy, and recurrence. By emulating the dynamic interactions among these mechanisms, CIO establishes an effective balance between global exploration and local exploitation, thereby enhancing convergence accuracy while reducing the risk of premature convergence to local optima. The performance of the proposed CIO algorithm is first assessed on a comprehensive collection of continuous benchmark functions encompassing unimodal, multimodal, separable, and non-separable optimization problems. Extensive numerical comparisons with several state-of-the-art metaheuristic algorithms demonstrate that CIO consistently obtains competitive or superior solution quality, faster convergence, and greater robustness across a wide range of Benchmark functions while maintaining satisfactory computational efficiency. To further demonstrate its practical applicability, CIO is employed to solve an optimal control problem (OCP) for breast cancer treatment. The proposed mathematical framework combines chemotherapy, immunotherapy, anti-cancer drug administration, and ketogenic diet intervention within a nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations describing tumor-immune interactions. The resulting OCP is discretized using a collocation scheme based on Boubaker scaling functions, yielding a finite-dimensional nonlinear programming problem that is efficiently solved using CIO. Numerical results show that the proposed hybrid framework effectively suppresses tumor growth, preserves healthy-cell populations, strengthens the immune response, and generates adaptive treatment strategies that achieve an appropriate balance between therapeutic efficacy and treatment-related toxicity. These findings demonstrate that CIO is not only an effective general-purpose optimization algorithm but also a reliable computational framework for solving complex biomedical OCPs.

papers.title: Persistent and compartmentalized T cell immunity in ALS.
papers.authors: Chen Z, Mansikkaviita J, Seitz C, Yazdani S, Lehikoinen J, Deeba E, Lovik A, Keszei M, Grönlund H, Laaksovirta H, Fang F, Tienari PJ, Ingre C, Andersson J.
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease increasingly linked to T cell responses, although the mechanisms driving T cell activation and disease progression remain unclear. Here we used single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling and imaging flow cytometry to identify long-lived intrathecal clonotypes and antigen-presenting cell-T cell complexes displaying features of immunological synapse formation, consistent with intrathecal antigen presentation. Higher frequencies of CD4 + effector, CD4 + regulatory and CD8 + T cells in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were associated with slower disease progression, whereas increased circulating CD4 + effector and regulatory T cells were associated with faster progression. T cell clonotypes shared between blood and CSF exhibited distinct transcriptional states. Finally, frequencies of cytomegalovirus-specific T cells in CSF and anticytomegalovirus serum antibodies were correlated with faster progression and shorter survival in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings reveal compartmentalized immune dynamics, largely contrasting protective intrathecal responses with harmful systemic activation.

papers.title: Integrative single-cell transcriptomic and metabolic profiling reveals lactate-driven glycolytic reprogramming and histone lactylation in colorectal cancer liver metastasis.
papers.authors: Liang Y, Deng X, Wang T, Chang X, Zhang Z.
papers.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion are hallmarks of cancer metastasis, but how tumor metabolism shapes the immune microenvironment during colorectal cancer (CRC) liver metastasis remains poorly understood. The role of E-cadherin (CDH1) beyond cell adhesion is unexplored. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, pseudotime trajectory inference, and in vivo/in vitro functional assays in primary and liver-metastatic CRC models. CellChat was used to map intercellular communication. Histone lactylation, ADAM10 activation, and CDH1 shedding were validated by biochemical and immunohistochemical assays. PGK1-driven glycolysis is upregulated in liver metastases and promotes metastatic progression. Elevated lactate induces histone H3K18 lactylation, activating ADAM10 expression. ADAM10 cleaves CDH1, releasing its soluble ectodomain. This fragment acts as a ligand for KLRG1 on T cells, driving exhaustion and immunosuppression. Cell-cell communication analysis confirmed CDH1-KLRG1 as a top differentially activated pathway in metastasis. Functionally, targeting PGK1 or blocking CDH1 shedding inhibits liver metastasis and restores T-cell function. We identify a metabolic-epigenetic-immune axis in which tumor glycolysis reprograms immunity via lactate-induced CDH1 shedding. Soluble CDH1 functions as an immunomodulatory signal, linking metabolic activity to T-cell exhaustion. This redefines CDH1 as a dual-function molecule and reveals actionable targets for metastatic CRC. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

papers.title: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma in rheumatoid arthritis express polyreactive and autoreactive BCRs binding protein modifications.
papers.authors: Euler N, Gonzalez-Sanchez AC, Clark E, Mildner H, Galesic M, Kemp A, Jangard M, Hellbacher E, Landegren N, Diaz-Gallo LM, Klareskog L, Malmström V, Baecklund E, Grönwall C.
papers.abstract: Background An important risk factor for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) development in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is high cumulated disease activity. B cell intrinsic factors and autoimmune processes may contribute, and we hypothesize that BCR autoreactivity may drive lymphomagenesis and/or lymphoma cell survival. RA is primarily associated with anti-citrullinated protein autoantibodies but patients can also have other anti-modified protein autoantibodies, e.g. towards malondialdehyde acetaldehyde (MDA/MAA) adducts which correlate with disease activity and inflammation. Here, we investigated DLBCL properties from RA patients with concurrent lymphoma by B-cell receptor (BCR) next generation sequencing and re-expression. Methods In total 22 RA-DLBCL patients were included from the Swedish AUTO-LYMPHOMA cohort. Tumour DNA was extracted from fixed tissues and full length VH/VL fragments were amplified by multiplex PCR and sequenced using Illumina. Computational analysis assessed clonal variations. Dominating sequences were synthesized and expressed as recombinant monoclonal antibodies for antigen binding analysis. Results Complete VH/VL lymphoma tissue sequences were generated from nine RA-DLBCL patients. Clonotype diversity within the tumour was generally low and the dominant paired heavy and light chain BCR sequences were obtained for six patients. For three patients, amino acid variations in the DLBCL clonotype indicated intra-clonal evolution. Two of six patients had tumour BCRs with few VH and VL somatic hypermutations (≤ 5 mismatches) while three had high mutations (> 15 VH or VL mismatches). No bias in VH/VL usage was detected. Six lymphoma BCRs from five patients were expressed as recombinant monoclonal antibodies and their binding to autoantigens was assessed by ELISA and a solid-phase microarray (> 400 antigens). All patient-derived lymphoma BCRs were CCP2 negative, but five bound MDA/MAA-protein. Three of these displayed polyreactive binding by in-house assays of which two further displayed strikingly broad polyreactivity on the antigen array. Importantly, for one patient, the lymphoma BCR had high specificity to MDA/MAA-protein, and another patient DLBCL-BCR had binding only to methylated protein. Conclusions The data suggest a possible link between polyreactivity and anti-MDA/MAA autoreactivity in RA-DLBCL lymphomagenesis. We hypothesize that high inflammation burden could increase antigen load which may trigger polyreactive and modified-protein B cell responses and/or maintain lymphoma cell survival.

papers.title: Oxidative stress-driven cellular heterogeneity in Knee Osteoarthritis: scRNA-seq pinpoints SPP1 and CYBA for diagnostic development.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Chi Y, Yin J, Yao J.
papers.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a progressive degenerative joint disease characterized by cartilage degeneration, synovial inflammation, and subchondral bone remodeling. Oxidative stress plays a critical role in KOA pathogenesis. This study aimed to identify oxidative stress-related hub genes by integrating single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with machine learning to uncover potential diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for KOA. ScRNA-seq data from KOA cartilage tissues were obtained from the GEO database to characterize cellular heterogeneity and identify disease-associated chondrocyte subsets. CellChat was used to analyze intercellular communication, and Monocle2 was applied to reconstruct cell differentiation trajectories. Oxidative stress activity at the single-cell level was evaluated using AUCell, while high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) was performed to identify oxidative stress-related gene modules. Candidate genes were screened using Venn analysis and further refined by LASSO regression, SVM-RFE, and XGBoost combined with SHAP analysis. Diagnostic performance was assessed, and biological relevance was explored through immune infiltration and pathway analyses. Experimental validation was conducted using qRT-PCR and western blot assays in H2O2-treated chondrocytes. InfC and ProFC were detected specifically in OA cartilage and exhibited high oxidative stress activity. InfC was enriched in inflammatory and immune-related pathways, whereas ProFC was associated with cell cycle regulation and extracellular matrix remodeling. Integrated hdWGCNA and machine-learning analyses consistently identified CYBA and SPP1 as candidate genes. The two-gene model achieved bootstrap-corrected AUCs of 0.937 and 0.825 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. qRT-PCR and western blot analyses further showed increased CYBA and SPP1 expression in H2O2-treated chondrocytes. Conclusion InfC and ProFC may represent OA-associated chondrocyte states characterized by enhanced oxidative stress, while CYBA and SPP1 may serve as candidate diagnostic biomarkers. Given the small cohort sizes and preliminary in vitro validation, these findings require confirmation in larger independent cohorts and functional studies.

papers.title: CDH1 loss remodels gene expression and lineage identity in human mammary epithelial cells.
papers.authors: Musick M, Ufondu CA, Rowland CE, Brown ME, Sottnik JL, Shackleford MT, Nesiba CS, Danis EP, Goodspeed AE, Zera R, Johnson AT, Schwertfeger KL, Nelson AC, Ostrander JH, Sikora MJ.
papers.abstract: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is a common subtype of breast cancer, molecularly defined by genetic loss of CDH1, and subsequent loss of cell adhesion protein E-cadherin, in ~95% of ILC. Though CDH1 loss occurs early in ILC oncogenesis, it is unclear how this facilitates transformation. We modeled early CDH1 loss using "normal" human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC), i.e., finite lifespan cells reflecting early hyperplasia, and targeted E-cadherin signaling using antibodies versus causing genetic CDH1 loss using siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9-knockout. Transcriptome analysis across four HMEC models showed that the mode of E-cadherin targeting is critical for the subsequent phenotype. Antibody-mediated inhibition of cell-cell contacts induced gene signatures of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), consistent with the role of E-cadherin suppression during the EMT process. Conversely, genetic CDH1 loss - as in ILC oncogenesis - repressed EMT signatures, and instead remodeled gene expression toward a luminal epithelial phenotype. RNA-seq, single cell transcriptomics, flow cytometry, microscopy, and ATAC-seq analyses support that CDH1 loss induces lineage remodeling to a luminal state, which is mirrored in transcriptomic analysis of clinical ILC precursor lesions. By isolating luminal versus basal cells prior to CDH1 knockout, we found that CDH1 loss led to remodeling of lineage identity in both populations, converging on a new lineage homeostasis with a luminal progenitor-like phenotype. Consistent with the shift to a luminal progenitor phenotype, CDH1 loss enhanced proliferative capacity over the finite lifespan of the HMECs, highlighting a feature of early CDH1 loss that may contribute to clonal advantage during tumor initiation. Moreover, CDH1 loss enhanced anoikis resistance, a defining feature of ILC cells. Our findings support that genetic loss of CDH1 in mammary epithelial cells induces transcriptional and phenotypic changes consistent with lineage identity remodeling toward a luminal progenitor-like state, which may underpin the mechanism by which early CDH1 loss mediates ILC oncogenesis.

papers.title: Schwann cell reprogramming and immune regulation in the cancer microenvironment.
papers.authors: Li H, Liu W, Liang J, Li Y, Pei J, Zhang C.
papers.abstract: Schwann cells are peripheral glia with established roles in nerve support and repair. In cancer, tumor-derived factors, inflammatory mediators and metabolic stress can redirect this repair program and generate tumor-associated Schwann cell (TASc) states. These cells are enriched around nerves and invasive fronts, where they have been linked to perineural invasion, extracellular matrix remodeling and changes in immune-cell localization and function. This Review summarizes recent work on the origin, recruitment and reprogramming of TAScs, with emphasis on molecular and cellular mechanisms rather than descriptive pathology alone. We discuss how transcriptional regulators, chemokines, neurotrophic factors, extracellular vesicles and metabolic pathways shape Schwann cell states in tumors, and how these states communicate with cancer cells, macrophages, T cells and natural killer cells. We also consider single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies that have refined TASc classification, while noting the limitations of marker-based annotation, model systems and cross-tumor extrapolation. Finally, we evaluate the potential use of TASc-associated programs as biomarkers and therapeutic entry points, particularly in tumors with perineural invasion or resistance to immunotherapy. A critical assessment of current evidence indicates that Schwann cell reprogramming is a context-dependent process that should be studied as part of the wider cellular organization of the cancer microenvironment.

papers.title: Spatial Proteomics Uncovers Immune Cell Neighborhoods and Tumor-Immune Interfaces in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Yeung J, Bai Y, Qiu H, Yeo YY, Chang Y, Ng MSF, Heij LR, Shah EA, Ma Q, Reiss D, Nolan G, Sivakumar S, Jiang S.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies with dismal prognosis and limited treatment options. The complex interplay between tumor cells and their microenvironment contributes significantly to treatment resistance, yet technological challenges have hindered comprehensive spatial characterization of immune components in PDAC tissues. Here, we performed high-dimensional spatial proteomics using multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI) to quantify 27 protein markers across tissues from twelve treatment-naïve PDAC patients who subsequently underwent adjuvant chemotherapy. We achieved confident single-cell phenotypic mapping of the PDAC ecosystem through deep-learning based segmentation and expert-validated phenotypic annotation. Our analysis revealed significant enrichment of immunosuppressive myeloid populations in patients who eventually experienced disease relapse. Conversely, cytotoxic CD8+ T cells were depleted in these relapse-prone tumors. Using spatial probabilistic topic modeling, we identified eight distinct cellular neighborhoods with unique compositions and functional states, including the enrichment of an immune suppressive neighborhood in relapsed patients. While immunogenic cell neighborhoods were present in both patient populations, analysis of the tumor-immune neighborhoods demonstrated altered functional marker expression profiles, suggesting distinct immune activation in patients who relapsed versus those who did not. Our findings provide a high-resolution spatial atlas of the PDAC immune landscape and identify prognostic microenvironmental signatures that may inform the development of novel immunotherapeutic strategies for this recalcitrant disease.

papers.title: Mining key differentially expressed genes and construction of a prognostic risk score model for colorectal cancer based on bioinformatics.
papers.authors: Liang L, Lin H, Jun L.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains the third most common malignancy and the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, with limited biomarkers available for accurate prognostic stratification. This study integrates multi-cohort transcriptomic data from four GEO datasets (GSE39582, GSE17536, GSE14333, GSE33113; n = 1123) and the TCGA-CRC cohort (n = 621) to identify key differentially expressed genes and construct a validated prognostic risk score model. Differential expression analysis using the limma framework identified 642 upregulated and 588 downregulated genes (|log2FC|>1, FDR<0.05). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) extracted hub genes from modules significantly correlated with overall survival. LASSO Cox regression then reduced the hub gene set to an eight-gene prognostic signature (MMP1, AURKA, TOP2A, CDH1, COL1A1, CLDN1, ETV4, CDX2) that stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups with significantly different survival outcomes (p < 0.001, log-rank test). The model achieved AUCs of 0.824, 0.796, and 0.768 for 1-, 3-, and 5-year overall survival in the training cohort and was validated in three independent datasets. High-risk patients exhibited immunosuppressive microenvironments (elevated M2 macrophages, Tregs) and increased resistance to standard chemotherapy agents. Integration of the risk score with clinical variables improved prognostic accuracy (C-index 0.812). These findings offer a robust bioinformatics-derived prognostic tool with implications for immunotherapy patient selection and personalized treatment planning in CRC.

papers.title: Histopathology-Based Spatial Profiling of Immune and Molecular Features Predicts Cancer Risk in Barrett's Esophagus Patients.
papers.authors: Ercan C, Pan X, Paulson TG, Stachler MD, Göknur Akarca F, Grady WM, Maley CC, Yuan Y.
papers.abstract: Barrett's esophagus (BE) patients require improved cancer risk stratification to identify high-risk individuals while reducing over-treatment in low-risk populations. BE evolution towards adenocarcinoma is likely driven by a combination of genomic and microenvironmental factors, suggesting the potential of predictive models that integrate both. Here, we developed BEACON (Barrett's Esophagus DNA content Abnormality and immune ecology for Cancer Outcome), a spatially aware framework integrating deep learning-based prediction of DNA content and immune architecture from routine histopathology. First, DACOR, a multi-instance learning model that predicts DNA content from histopathology, was trained using 777 BE biopsies with flow cytometry-based DNA content data scanned at two institutions, and it demonstrated strong performance across both validation and test datasets for DNA content abnormality prediction. Patients classified as DNA content abnormal by DACOR demonstrated increased cancer progression. Complementary models for cell classification and tissue segmentation enabled spatial immune ecology metric computations. Abnormal regions exhibited increased lymphoplasmacytic inflammation versus normal regions. Among patients with DNA content abnormality, cancer progressors exhibited increased plasma cell clustering adjacent to abnormal epithelium compared to non-progressors. Finally, a logistic regression model was developed that integrated molecular, immune ecological, and epithelial morphology features for cancer risk stratification. The integrated risk classification model stratified DNA content abnormal patients into high- and low-risk groups that corresponded with progression and patient survival. Overall, BEACON spatially integrates molecular abnormality with immune ecology to stratify BE patients by cancer progression risk using routine pathology images.

papers.title: Immune-Related Biomarkers and an Exploratory Prognostic Signature in Biliary Tract and Gallbladder Cancer.
papers.authors: Zhou Z, Yang Y, Yang Z, Liu S, Gong W.
papers.abstract: Gallbladder cancer is an aggressive biliary tract malignancy associated with poor prognosis and limited molecularly guided treatment options. Chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation play central roles in gallbladder carcinogenesis; however, reproducible computational workflows for identifying immune-related biomarkers remain limited. This study describes an integrated bioinformatic workflow for identifying immune-related differentially expressed genes (IRDEGs) and developing an exploratory prognostic gene signature. Differential expression analysis was performed using dataset-specific R-based workflows, and differentially expressed genes were intersected with immune-related gene sets obtained from ImmPort, InnateDB, and the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB). Gene Ontology, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, and gene set enrichment analyses were conducted to characterize biological functions and signaling pathways. Protein-protein interaction networks were constructed using STRING and Cytoscape; immune-cell infiltration was estimated using CIBERSORT; and prognostic genes were identified through sequential univariate, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox, and multivariable Cox regression analyses. The analysis identified 824 consensus differentially expressed genes, including 312 IRDEGs. These genes were significantly enriched in inflammatory and immune-regulatory pathways, including IL6/JAK/STAT3, nuclear factor of kappa light chain enhancer (NF-κB), Toll-like receptor, and chemokine signaling pathways. CXCL8, IL1B, MMP9, TLR2, S100A8, and S100A9 were identified as key hub genes. Immune-cell infiltration analysis revealed a markedly altered tumor immune microenvironment. An exploratory five-gene prognostic signature comprising CXCL8, S100A9, IL16, MMP9, and CD36 successfully stratified patients according to overall survival risk. This integrated workflow provides a reproducible framework for identifying immune-related biomarkers and developing exploratory prognostic signatures in gallbladder cancer. However, independent clinical cohorts and experimental validation are required before these findings can be translated into clinical applications.

papers.title: Bulk RNA sequencing deconvolution of early-onset pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma identifies cancer-associated fibroblast subsets associated with survival and tumor microenvironment composition.
papers.authors: Dam N, Steketee MFB, Strijk G, de Koning W, Hawinkels LJAC, Kemp V, van Eijck CHJ, Kim Y, van Eijck CWF, van Os BW.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal cancer characterized by a high abundance of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which influence therapy response, tumor biology and tumor aggressiveness. CAFs are a heterogeneous cell type and previous single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) of PDAC tumors identified three main CAF subtypes: myofibroblastic, inflammatory and antigen-presenting CAFs (myCAF, iCAF, apCAF, respectively). However, scRNAseq on large patient cohorts is often not feasible due to costs and technical constraints. Therefore, bulk RNAseq deconvolution can be used to computationally infer cell types within the tumor microenvironment. Here, Statescope deconvolution was used to identify different cell types of the tumor microenvironment within an early-onset PDAC cohort, comprising 74 patients aged under 60. Three CAF states were detected (iCAFs, myCAFs and desmoplastic CAFs), and their correlations with microenvironmental components, mutational signatures and survival were explored. iCAFs were associated with classical-like tumor cells, whereas myCAFs and desmoplastic CAFs were correlated with basal-like tumor cells. Desmoplastic CAFs are associated with inflammatory granulocytes/neutrophils, while negatively associating with monocyte-derived macrophages and immature/transitional B cells. No associations were observed between mutational signatures and the abundance of CAF and epithelial tumor subtypes. Interestingly, a high abundance of CAFs, and specifically increased iCAF abundance, was associated with improved survival. Deconvolution of bulk RNA sequencing data, followed by its integration with clinical and biological parameters, provides insights into the heterogeneity of CAF subpopulations in the tumor microenvironment of early-onset PDAC patients and explores potential associations with clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Leptin drives osteoarthritis pain through sensory neuron reprogramming independent of cartilage signaling.
papers.authors: Welhaven HD, Truchan EK, Lenz KL, Andoko BA, Alhadi MA, Mazzucco MR, Villa RE, Oestreich AK, Zhang B, Orange DE, Lesnak JB, Price TJ, Guilak F, Collins KH.
papers.abstract: Objective Pain in osteoarthritis (OA) is often discordant with structural joint damage, particularly in obesity, where adipose-derived signals may drive nociception independently of cartilage pathology. Leptin has been demonstrated to be necessary, but not sufficient, to drive obesity-associated OA. Here, we tested the hypothesis that leptin mediates OA-associated pain through sensory neuron reprogramming rather than chondrocyte-intrinsic signaling, suggesting a fat-sensory nerve axis. Design Male and female chondrocyte-specific leptin receptor knockout mice (Aggrecan-CreERT2;LepRfl/fl) and constitutive leptin-deficient (Ob/Ob), heterozygous (Ob/+), and wild-type (WT) mice were challenged with destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) to induce OA. Pain-related behaviors, joint pathology, serum cytokines, and lumbar dorsal root ganglia (DRG) transcriptomes were assessed. Human DRG cultures treated with leptin underwent transcriptomic profiling. Leptin and leptin receptor expression was investigated in human infrapatellar fat pad and synovium single-cell datasets. Results Chondrocyte-specific deletion of the leptin receptor did not alter structural joint pathology or pain. In contrast, complete leptin deficiency (Ob/Ob) produced more severe structural damage following DMM while markedly reducing pain sensitivity. Comparing DMM limbs of Ob/+ animals to those of Ob/Ob animals, Modified Mankin score was 24.95% higher (95% CI 2.02-11.49) indicating greater structural damage, while pressure-pain thresholds were 37.5% higher (95% CI, 23.92-54.46g), indicating attenuated pain, together demonstrating dissociation between structural pathology and nociception. Circulating cytokines did not differ by genotype between Ob/+ and Ob/Ob mice, providing no systemic inflammatory signature corresponding to their divergent pain phenotypes. Mouse DRGs exhibited genotype-associated transcriptional differences, with Ob/+ DRGs enriched for lipid metabolism, eicosanoid, and inflammatory programs, whereas Ob/Ob DRGs were characterized by cytoskeletal remodeling and altered neuronal signaling. In human DRG cultures, acute leptin exposure was associated with enrichment of neuronal and nociceptor-associated transcriptional programs, whereas vehicle-treated cultures were enriched for inflammatory signaling. Human infrapatellar fat pad and synovium transcriptomic data demonstrated adipocyte-enriched leptin expression and broad leptin receptor distribution across stromal, vascular, immune, and adipocyte populations. Conclusions In mice, leptin contributes to OA pain independently of chondrocyte-intrinsic signaling and structural disease severity. These findings identify leptin-associated neuronal programs linked to nociceptor sensitization and support further investigation of adipose-joint-sensory neuron signaling as a mediator of obesity-associated OA pain.

papers.title: A putative oxidoreductase, Rv1714 from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, predicted as a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase, exhibits a pro-inflammatory response.
papers.authors: Shiraz M, Singh S, Andole S, Biswas D, Fatima AW, Khan N, Akif M.
papers.abstract: Oxidoreductases are a class of enzymes that transfer electrons in various biological pathways and reactions, at the expense of cellular NADPH/NADH. Because oxidoreductases are involved in numerous energy metabolism pathways, many of these enzymes have been identified as potential drug targets. Although oxidoreductases have been implicated in energy metabolism pathways and are crucial for the survival and pathogenicity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), their comprehensive characterization remains limited. In the present study, one uncharacterized and putative oxidoreductase, Rv1714, was identified in the H37Rv proteome. This putative oxidoreductase was conserved across pathogenic and opportunistic mycobacterial species and was predicted to be a virulence factor essential for the pathogenicity. Rv1714 displayed homology with the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family. The recombinant Rv1714 was purified to homogeneity, and its structural properties were explored using CD and fluorescence spectroscopies, as well as bioinformatics tools. The sequence and structural homologies revealed the characteristic features and conservation of the active site with the SDR family of proteins. Possible substrates were explored using docking, simulation, and MMPBSA calculations. Furthermore, in vitro studies using macrophage cell lines demonstrate that recombinant Rv1714 significantly enhances the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL1β, TNF-α, and IL-6, suggesting that Rv1714 may play a critical role in modulating the host's innate immune response during infection. The stimulation of these cytokines is associated with the activation of the NF-κB pathway. Altogether, this is the first report on the putative oxidoreductase Rv1714 of M.tb, highlighting its structural features and its key immune-modulatory function involved in shaping host inflammatory responses during infection.
